title: Alkyl halides: SN1, SN2, E1, E2
note: Methyl and primary halides favor SN2; tertiary halides give SN1/E1 with weak nucleophiles and E2 with strong bases. Strong, bulky bases push E2. Polar aprotic solvents speed SN2; polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation for SN1. Good leaving groups are weak bases: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ ≫ F⁻.

read.title: Choosing among four paths
text: An alkyl halide meeting a nucleophile or base can react in four main ways. In SN2, the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group in one step, so the carbon's configuration inverts. Crowding blocks that backside approach, so SN2 is fastest at methyl and primary carbons and fails at tertiary ones. Polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO help, because they leave anionic nucleophiles unsolvated and reactive.

In SN1, the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation, and the nucleophile adds afterward to either face, which scrambles stereochemistry. The rate depends only on the substrate, and tertiary halides react fastest because they form the most stable cations. Polar protic solvents stabilize the ions. E1 shares the same carbocation and simply loses a proton instead.

E2 is a one-step elimination in which a base removes a hydrogen anti-periplanar to the leaving group as the π bond forms. Strong bases favor it, especially with secondary and tertiary halides. Small bases such as ethoxide give mainly the more substituted Zaitsev alkene; bulky bases such as tert-butoxide pull off the more accessible hydrogen and give the less substituted Hofmann alkene.
A practical summary: identify the substrate class, then ask whether the reagent is a strong base, a good nucleophile, or neither.

q.q: Why does SN2 fail at tertiary carbons?
o: The leaving group is too good

o: Its bulk favors the more accessible hydrogen
